draft.title: Young's double slit experiment
card: In Young's experiment, light from one source passes through two narrow slits close together. The two beams overlap on a screen and make a pattern of bright and dark bands called fringes.
Interference makes the bands. Where the waves arrive in phase, they add to give a bright fringe. Where they arrive out of phase, they cancel to give a dark fringe.
Interference is a wave behaviour. A stream of simple particles would make two bright patches, so the fringes showed that light behaves as a wave.

Bright fringes follow d sin θ = mλ. Here d is the slit separation, θ is the angle from the centre line, m is the order (0, 1, 2 and so on) and λ is the wavelength. Larger λ or smaller d spreads the fringes further apart.
draft.remember: Bright and dark fringes come from interference, so light behaves as a wave.

a.q: What does the pattern of bright and dark fringes in Young's experiment show about light?
opts: It can interfere, so it behaves as a wave
It travels in straight lines, so it is a particle stream
It is bent by the slits, so it has mass
It travels at different speeds through each slit
a.why: Bright and dark fringes come from waves adding and cancelling, which is interference. A stream of simple particles would give two bright patches, not alternating bands, so the straight-line particle idea does not fit.
a.clue: Which behaviour makes waves add and cancel?

b.q: Mia shines red laser light through a double slit and sees fringes on a screen. She swaps to a blue laser, which has a shorter wavelength, and changes nothing else. What happens to the fringe spacing?
opts: The fringes stay the same distance apart
b.why: From d sin θ = mλ, with d fixed, a smaller λ gives a smaller sin θ for each order m. The fringes therefore sit closer together. They do not disappear, because blue light still interferes.
b.clue: With d fixed, what happens to sin θ when λ gets smaller?

a.best: It can interfere, so it behaves as a wave
